annotations.keyFindings: In routine services only 30 to 52 percent of referred women attended more than half of the sessions; travel time, caring responsibilities and milder symptoms were the predictors most often reported.
annotations.limitations: Heterogeneous attendance definitions; no study linked reported barriers to recorded attendance.

annotations.keyFindings: Of 1,204 referred women, 41 percent attended the first session and 23 percent four or more; non-attendance was commoner under 25, beyond 20 kilometres and with interpreter need.
annotations.limitations: One hospital; reasons not recorded; postnatal women only.

annotations.keyFindings: Childcare (46 percent), group embarrassment (31 percent) and clashing class times (29 percent) were the commonest barriers; non-attenders replied far less often.
annotations.limitations: 38 percent response, English only, answers not linked to attendance.

annotations.keyFindings: After evening and online classes were added, first-session attendance rose from 44 to 63 percent, most among mothers of young children.
annotations.limitations: Before-after comparison with a simultaneous fall in waiting time.

annotations.keyFindings: Completion of four or more sessions ranged from 19 to 44 percent across five services.
annotations.limitations: Undated internal report; counting methods, months and service selection not described; not rated.

annotations.keyFindings: Women needing an interpreter were about half as likely to attend a first appointment (prevalence ratio 0.52) after adjustment for age and distance.
annotations.limitations: Interpreter need recorded inconsistently; two hospitals.

annotations.keyFindings: Group and individual training gave similar attendance (71 and 74 percent) and similar improvement in trial volunteers living near the hospital.
annotations.limitations: Volunteers with easy access; attendance far above routine services.

claims.text: In a review of 1,204 referrals, 41 percent attended the first session and non-attendance was commoner in women under 25, living over 20 kilometres away or needing an interpreter.
claims.passage: Forty-one percent attended the first session and 23 percent attended four or more of six sessions.
claims.interpretation: Planning values for attendance and candidate record-based factors.

claims.text: Among women who replied to a postal survey, childcare was the most common barrier to pelvic floor classes.
claims.passage: Childcare was the most common barrier (46 percent), followed by embarrassment about discussing symptoms in a group (31 percent)
claims.interpretation: Barriers must be asked directly; non-attenders reply less, so the survey needs reminders and linkage.

claims.text: Adding evening and online classes was followed by a rise in first-session attendance from 44 to 63 percent.
claims.passage: first-session attendance rose from 44 to 63 percent
claims.interpretation: Class timing is a plausible modifiable factor; the before-after design limits inference.

claims.text: Women who needed an interpreter were about half as likely to attend their first appointment.
claims.passage: Women who needed an interpreter were about half as likely to attend their first appointment (prevalence ratio 0.52, 95 percent CI 0.41 to 0.66)
claims.interpretation: Language must be measured and the survey translated.

claims.text: No study linked patient-reported barriers to recorded attendance.
claims.passage: none linked patient-reported barriers to recorded attendance
claims.interpretation: Linking survey answers to attendance records would fill a gap, if permitted.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level; one undated service report is left unrated. Attendance at group pelvic floor classes in routine services is far below trial attendance, and records-based studies point to age, distance and interpreter need, while surveys point to childcare, embarrassment and class times. Nobody has linked reported barriers to recorded attendance, and surveys miss non-attenders. Evening and online classes were followed by higher attendance in one service, but waiting times fell at the same time.
gradeRationale: Single-service observational studies and one survey with low response; consistent direction for distance, language and childcare but serious risk of bias and indirect trial evidence.
summary: Seven retrieved records appraised, one undated report unrated; five source-derived claims; overall certainty low.
